fundamental.thesis: AWL Agri Business (formerly Adani Wilmar) is India's largest branded edible oil and packaged food company, operating the Fortune brand across a 2.6 million-outlet distribution network, with a fast-scaling Food & FMCG segment crossing ₹1,700 cr revenue (+22% YoY) and a nascent but high-growth Quick Commerce channel (+56% YoY). Q1FY27 revenue grew +18% YoY to ₹20,048 cr and PAT recovered sharply +48% YoY to ₹351 cr (1.8% margin), but the multi-quarter trajectory carries important caveats: revenue growth has decelerated from +24% (FY25) → +10% (Q3FY26) → partial recovery at +18%, gross margins have contracted from 11.8% (FY25) to ~10.5% (FY26), and critically the core edible oil segment grew just 2% by volume in Q1FY27 with 11% price/mix doing the heavy lifting — a classic demand-quality warning from the FMCG Sector Card. At 20.72× trailing P/E (vs sector card norm of 40–65× for FMCG) and EV/EBITDA of 8.98× (P8 percentile vs 473 universe peers, a −62% discount to the 23.3× median), AWL screens unambiguously cheap, but the deep discount is structural: commodity-linked PAT margins of ~1.8%, extreme financial leverage (D/E 10.62), and a residual Adani Group governance discount even post-rebrand collectively justify a persistent valuation haircut. The primary risk is extreme leverage (D/E 10.62) married to sub-2% PAT margins, where rising crude ($90.41 — a headwind on crude-derivative inputs) and any further edible oil volume stagnation could rapidly erode earnings, compounded by FII sustained net-selling and MIDCAP-tier liquidity constraints limiting institutional re-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Patanjali Foods is India's largest edible oils company (formerly Ruchi Soya), with a fast-growing FMCG overlay spanning biscuits, nutrition, and home/personal care under the Patanjali brand — but edible oils still account for roughly 70%+ of revenues, making this a commodity-FMCG hybrid rather than a pure compounder, and that matters critically for how to frame the valuation. Q1FY27 delivered record revenue of ₹11,337 cr (+29.3% YoY, accelerating from +20.9% in Q2FY26) and PAT of ₹336 cr (+86.1% YoY), but underlying quality is deteriorating: gross margin compressed from 15.26% (Q2FY26) to 13.42% (Q1FY27), EBITDA margin fell from 6.2% to 4.8%, and PAT margin contracted to 3.0% — a persistent multi-quarter contraction signal that runs counter to the top-line acceleration. At trailing P/E 25.43×, the stock screens cheap versus the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–60×, but the discount is structurally warranted by the commodity-heavy business mix; EV/EBITDA of 25× (P55 vs broad-market peers) and P/E peer rank of P32 both point to fair value rather than genuine mispricing, and the sector card's own caution — 'cheap FMCG usually means a structural problem' — applies directly here. fundamental.thesis: Tata Consumer Products is India's second-largest branded foods-and-beverages company, with leading positions in tea (Tata Tea, Tetley) and salt (Tata Salt), supplemented by an inorganic expansion into nutrition and adjacent FMCG via Capital Foods, Soulfull, and Organic India acquisitions. Q1FY27 revenue grew +11.9% YoY to ₹5,349 cr — a meaningful deceleration from +15.0% in Q3FY26 — though PAT surged +28.8% YoY to ₹427 cr (margin 8.0% vs 7.0% a year ago), powered by lower tea input costs and gross-margin expansion from 40.1% to 42.7%; volume growth in the India business was ~13%, solid but to be weighed against the sector card's caution on >10% volume claims. At a trailing P/E of 60.51× — at the upper bound of the FMCG benchmark range of 40–60× and ranked P78 among broad-market peers — the stock screens as expensive even near its 52-week low; however, a forward P/E of 41.78× (31% below trailing) signals the market is pricing in a meaningful earnings step-up from acquisition integration and tea-cost tailwinds. The principal risk is sustained revenue growth deceleration toward sub-10% alongside a reported Debt/Equity of 12.16 (reflecting heavy acquisition financing), which leaves the stock highly exposed to multiple compression if earnings delivery disappoints or high-rate conditions pressure interest coverage.

IndiaMART runs India's largest online B2B marketplace and is profitable and cash-rich: it holds ₹3,234 cr of cash and investments, and cash from operations is about 1.5x reported profit. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 9.7% YoY to ₹429 cr, slowing from +12% a year ago and +13% in FY26, and profit rose about 9.6% to ₹91 cr. EBITDA margin improved from 33% to 37%, but the number of paying suppliers fell 2% YoY to 217k. Deferred revenue grew 16% and collections grew 9%, which still points to growth around 10%. Because this is a profitable platform, I graded it mainly on EV/EBITDA (18.1x) and trailing P/E (27.1x, forward 20.7x), which sit about 22% below the broad-market median (around P35) and are modest for a debt-free platform with a 20.7% ROE, so valuation is fair to slightly cheap. The biggest risk is that paying suppliers keep shrinking, so growth relies only on price hikes and the business stalls at high single-digit growth, all in a risk-off market with a macro headwind for consumer discretionary names.

fundamental.thesis: Balkrishna Industries (BKT) is India's dominant specialty off-highway tire (OHT) manufacturer — serving agricultural, industrial, and construction segments globally with ~6% global OHT market share — with heavy export dependence on Europe and a capital-intensive manufacturing model that makes EV/EBITDA the primary valuation yardstick. fundamental.thesis: Jubilant FoodWorks is India's dominant QSR operator as master franchisee for Domino's Pizza (~2,562 domestic stores, 3,636 total group), with strong own-channel moats — 70% own-app order penetration, 17mn monthly active users, and 31mn loyalty members. Q1FY27 revenue grew 14.1% YoY to ₹2,570cr but has decelerated from Q4FY26's +19.3%, while PAT margin has contracted materially from 6.0% (H1FY26) to 3.9% (Q1FY27) driven by ₹120cr/quarter in finance costs (~23% of EBITDA, predominantly Ind AS 116 lease liabilities) and an effective tax-rate jump from 25.3% to 31.8%; the critical sector KPI — Domino's India LFL — has slowed from 7.5% in FY25 to 6.5% in FY26 to 5.0% in Q3FY26, signalling volume pressure even as footprint expansion continues. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (Ind AS 116 makes P/E structurally elevated and less comparable), at 21.94× the stock sits at the sector P50 — fair — though trailing P/E of 83.7× at P82 vs peers and a -7.9% cut to next-FY EPS estimates over 90 days warns that the forward P/E of 52.1× recovery narrative is at risk. The biggest risk is sustained LFL deceleration toward or below management's 5–7% guidance floor, which in a premium-multiple franchise historically triggers the 25–40% de-ratings the sector card warns of, compounded by a recent senior management change filing and the permanent loss of the Dunkin' development rights as a growth avenue.

Godrej Properties is one of India's largest branded residential developers and its fastest land buyer, working asset-light through JVs and joint development deals across MMR, Bengaluru, NCR, Pune and Hyderabad; its market share doubled from 2.4% in CY21 to 4.8% in CY25. As the sector card notes, reported P&L lags the real business by years, so the key operating number is FY26 bookings: ₹34,171 cr, up 16% YoY, slower than Q3FY26's +55% quarterly print. Collections were ₹19,965 cr (+17%) and land deals added ₹42,100 cr (+59%). H1FY27 revenue more than doubled (+107.8% to ₹2,441 cr), but PAT fell 49.8% to ₹495 cr (12.6% margin), and roughly ₹309 cr of that profit is a non-cash fair-value gain, so underlying earnings are much weaker. Operating cash flow was negative ₹724 cr and net debt rose to about ₹8,111 cr from ₹7,607 cr in Q1. The pack has no Q2FY27 bookings figure, which is the number that matters most. I graded valuation on P/B plus pre-sales, not P/E, as the card advises: P/B of 2.68x for a 10% ROE, and a market cap of about 1.5x FY26 bookings, looks fair, not cheap. The stock sits at 25% of its 52-week range, and analysts' next-year earnings estimates are rising (+14.6% over 90 days). The biggest risk is that aggressive land buying is outrunning cash generation (debt-service coverage of 0.47x, interest coverage of 1.08x) just as rates and risk appetite turn against a RISK_OFF real estate tape.

fundamental.thesis: Authum Investment & Infrastructure (AIIL) is a leveraged NBFC-type investment holding company that earns income primarily from equities, lending, and capital gains — reflected in its exceptionally high PAT margins (74–94% in normal quarters). Q1FY27 showed a revenue recovery to ₹1,486 cr (+21.4% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,108 cr (+17.5% YoY), reversing the severe FY26 collapse (revenue -43%, PAT -55.8%), but the Q1FY27 EPS collapsed 76.5% YoY as paid-up share capital was inflated ~5× (₹16.98 cr → ₹84.92 cr), indicating a large equity dilution event that masks per-share value destruction. Valuation yardstick used: P/B + ROE per the sector card for lenders — trailing P/E of 8.95× sits at P5 vs 473 peers (deeply cheap on P/E) but P/B of 2.91× with ROE of 13.1% is borderline by the P/B<1.5/ROE>12% cheap threshold; the apparent P/E cheapness likely reflects a justified market discount for extreme D/E of 24.59 and volatile, lumpy earnings. The single biggest risk is that the D/E of 24.59 makes the book acutely vulnerable to mark-to-market shocks or a credit cycle turn, compounded by the 5× dilution overhang and an NSE volume-movement clarification request on 15 Sep 2026 — a surveillance flag that adds governance uncertainty.

Aditya Birla Sun Life AMC is a mid-sized mutual fund manager whose earnings track equity AUM and fund flows, so it moves with the market. The latest results we could read are for Q1 FY27; the Q2/H1 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-21 were not extracted, so the most recent quarter is missing. In Q1 FY27, revenue from operations rose only 3.5% YoY to ₹463 cr, down from about +9.5% in FY26 and +10.4% in 9M FY26. PAT grew 11.7% to ₹309 cr, but a large ₹162 cr of other income (mostly treasury gains) helped, which flatters the 66.9% PAT margin and the 90.7% EBITDA margin. Our valuation yardstick would be P/AUM-linked earnings, but no AUM data was provided, so we fell back to P/E plus P/B and ROE: trailing P/E of 34.6× is near the broad-market median (P48), and P/B of 8.3× is backed by a 25% ROE, so we rate it fair. The stock is at 99.4% of its 52-week range while analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by about 15.6% over 90 days. The snapshot also has errors: a 214% dividend yield, a 1.58 debt/equity ratio that doesn't fit an asset-light AMC, and a mean target of ₹1,103 labelled '+30%' when the price is near ₹1,165. Together these leave little room for error and keep conviction low.

fundamental.thesis: Aptus Value Housing Finance is a mid-sized affordable-housing lender in South India that makes small-ticket loans to self-employed and informal-income borrowers, and earns a high return on assets (ROA 7.76% in FY26). Growth is slowing from +23-30% in FY26 to +17%, and AUM growth was only 12.2% in FY26, below Aptus's historical pace. Using P/B against ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, 2.69x book for a 20.1% ROE looks cheap. Trailing P/E of 14.5x (forward 10.5x) is also below the 18-28x NBFC range and sits at P13 vs the broad market. The main risk is asset quality: GNPA rose from 1.19% to 1.42% and NNPA from 0.90% to 1.07% while provision coverage is thin at about 25%, and the company keeps selling loans to ARCs at a loss. Q2FY27 results are due on 4 Nov and could confirm or ease this trend.

fundamental.thesis: CAMS is India's largest registrar and transfer agent for mutual funds (~70% market share), a capital-light quasi-monopoly whose revenue is directly proportional to equity AUM and transaction volumes — it earns a toll on India's mutual-fund ecosystem. Q1FY27 showed a clear re-acceleration after a soft FY26 mid-stretch: revenue grew +11.5% YoY to ₹395 cr and PAT grew +17.4% YoY to ₹128 cr, reversing the Q2FY26 PAT contraction of -6.1%; PAT margin expanded to a fresh high of 32.4% from a 29.6% trough, while EBITDA margin also nudged up — the multi-quarter direction is now firmly improving even if growth remains below FY25's stellar +25% revenue and +33% PAT pace. Valuation yardstick used: EV/EBITDA and forward P/E for this capital-light services model (P/B is inflated by high ROE and not the right lens); trailing P/E of 43.6× sits above the broad-market median of 35.2× (P64 rank), EV/EBITDA of 27.6× is a modest 18% premium to the 23.3× median (P60 rank), and forward P/E of 32.2× — a meaningful 26% discount to trailing — reflects priced-in earnings growth from a high-ROE (38.7%) platform; grade: fair, near a 52-week high (84% of range) which limits near-term entry margin of safety. The biggest near-term risk is the RISK_OFF macro regime: AUM growth has already decelerated from 24% (FY25) to 16% (Q2FY26), FII net outflows of -₹44,013 cr over 30 days threaten equity AUM, and a sustained market correction would compress CAMS fee revenue with no offsetting diversification — the D/E of 4.86 (likely Ind AS 116 lease liabilities, but worth monitoring) adds a secondary watch item.

fundamental.thesis: Can Fin Homes is a mid-size Housing Finance Company (HFC) and Canara Bank subsidiary, focused on affordable housing (83% of portfolio) across 21 states through 250 branches — a niche lender with institutional parentage and a structurally low-cost origination model. PAT growth has re-accelerated from -4.3% YoY in Q1FY26 through +18% in Q2FY26 and +27% in FY26, sustaining at +20.2% in Q1FY27 (₹268 cr); H1FY27 PAT margin expanded to 24.4% from 22.4% in Q1FY26, and GNPA collapsed from 6.71% (Q1FY26) to 0.90% (H1FY27) while disbursement growth surged to 29% YoY in Q1FY27 — a leading signal for portfolio acceleration — though NIM has edged down from 3.93% (FY26) to 3.81% (Q1FY27), using the sector-card P/B+ROE yardstick for lenders, P/B of 1.74× against ROE of 17.15% grades clearly cheap (below the 1.5× threshold but with materially above-12% ROE), with the stock sitting at P5 in broad-market peers, near its 52-week low, and forward P/E of 8.23× below trailing 9.19× confirming further earnings growth priced in. The biggest risk to this thesis is NIM erosion accelerating: deposit repricing typically lags EBLR-linked asset yield cuts in an easing cycle, the LCR has already fallen from 250% in Q1FY27 to 100% at H1FY27 (the regulatory floor), and ISCR of 1.51 leaves a thin interest-coverage buffer if borrowing costs prove sticky.

fundamental.thesis: Choice International is a diversified mid-cap financial services company with broking (59% of revenue), advisory (27%), and NBFC lending (13%), managing ₹62,226cr in client broking assets and 12.94 lakh demat accounts across equity, insurance, and wealth segments. Q1FY27 revenue grew 32% YoY to ₹310cr — an acceleration from +16.6% in Q1FY26 — with PAT rising 26.4% to ₹61cr and PAT margin expanding to 19.6% from a trough of 14.7% in Q3FY25; insurance policies sold surged 73% YoY, though wealth AUM grew a tepid 4% and demat account additions moderated to +13%. At a trailing P/E of 63× (vs NBFC median of 18–28× and AMC/broking P/B+ROE framework suggesting fair value closer to 3–4× book for a 16.2% ROE), the stock ranks at the P80–P91 percentile within the broad market, making it clearly expensive regardless of the growth premium applied; the Q3FY25 revenue row (₹2,093cr) appears to be a data anomaly inconsistent with the FY25 full-year figure of ₹910cr and is excluded from trajectory conclusions. The single biggest fundamental risk is the 59% broking revenue concentration, which creates acute earnings sensitivity to equity market activity — in the current RISK_OFF regime with 30-day FII outflows of ₹44,013cr, bearish NIFTY 100 momentum, and market breadth collapsed to 18% above the 50-DMA, broking volumes and fee income are under material cyclical pressure.

Aavas Financiers is a mid-sized affordable-housing lender focused on self-employed, low-to-middle-income borrowers in semi-urban areas, with 443 branches across 15 states and AUM of ₹24,801 cr. Revenue growth has slowed steadily from +15.7% in Q1FY26 to about +10.3% in Q2FY27: H1 revenue was ₹1,445 cr less Q1's ₹709 cr, which gives ₹736 cr for Q2, against ₹667 cr a year ago. Q2 profit was about ₹182 cr, up roughly 11% and slower than Q1's +23%, while the profit margin held steady at about 24.7% and gross bad loans were stable at 1.24%. Following the sector card, I graded valuation on price-to-book versus return on equity rather than P/E: 2.3x book for a 13.9% ROE is fair, not cheap. The forward P/E of 12.6x against a trailing 17.9x points to expected earnings growth, but the 'cheap vs peers' tag compares against the whole market, not housing lenders, so I give it little weight. The main risk is that growth keeps slowing toward single digits. Active loan accounts also fell from 275.8k to 255.6k, which is worth checking against the transcript at the 2 Nov analyst meet.

fundamental.thesis: Capri Global Capital is a mid-sized diversified NBFC whose consolidated AUM grew 62% YoY to Rs 43,878 cr. Gold loans, up 102% YoY, are now about 48% of AUM, with MSME, affordable housing and construction finance making up most of the rest. Q2FY27 net total income was Rs 1,085 cr (+58.9% YoY) and PAT was a record Rs 418 cr (+77.3% YoY), a 38.5% PAT margin; growth is steady rather than accelerating, with AUM growth at 62.3% vs 62.0% last quarter. Spread on advances rose to 8.3% from 7.9% QoQ, cost-to-income fell to 41.4% from 44.0% QoQ, and RoAE rose to 21.6% from 19.1% QoQ, so operating quality is still improving. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the lender yardstick, rather than P/E. A P/B of 2.96x for TTM ROE of 16.5% (latest-quarter RoAE 21.6%) is fair, not cheap. The forward P/E of 12.2x is well below the trailing 21.8x, and analysts raised estimates 7.7% over 90 days. But the stock is at 95% of its 52-week range, so much of the good news looks priced in. The main concern is that fast growth is eating into the safety buffers. Provision coverage on Stage 3 loans fell from 43.2% to 33.3% in one quarter, net Stage 3 rose from 0.6% to 0.8%, and standalone capital adequacy (CRAR) dropped from 24.7% to 22.7%, all while gold-price exposure is rising.

fundamental.thesis: United Breweries is India's largest beer maker, built on Kingfisher and backed by Heineken. Its premium brands (Heineken Silver, Kingfisher Ultra) are growing fastest, but sales depend on state-by-state excise and distribution rules. In Q2FY27 net sales grew 23.7% YoY, up from 10.0% in Q1, on 16% volume growth and 38% premium volume growth, and EBITDA margin rose 480bps to 11.9%. PAT was ₹135 cr, up 190.9% YoY, but last year's quarter was weak, so H1 PAT growth of +31% is the fairer read, and Q1 PAT was actually down 9.6%. The trend table's 'accelerating' signal partly compares quarters against the full FY26 year, so I put less weight on it. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E against peers, as the FMCG card suggests: trailing P/E is 84x against a sector median of 51.5x (P92), forward P/E is 46x (P83) and EV/EBITDA is 47.9x (P83), which is expensive even for this premium sector, even with the stock near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that the multiple shrinks if analysts keep cutting estimates (next-FY EPS down 6.7% over 90 days) or if a state changes excise or distribution policy. The ₹752 cr CCI penalty still pending at the Supreme Court is a smaller overhang.

fundamental.thesis: Billionbrains Garage Ventures (Groww) runs one of India's largest retail investing platforms: broking, mutual-fund distribution, an AMC (State Street now holds 22.94% of the economic interest) and a fast-growing lending and margin-funding book. So it is best judged as a capital-markets platform on P/E against growth and P/B against ROE, not as a bank. H1FY27 revenue rose 56.2% YoY to ₹3,003 cr and PAT rose 71.8% to ₹1,460 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹1,502 cr (+47% YoY on a weak, -9.5% base) and PAT of about ₹725 cr (+54%), so growth slowed from +66% in Q1. The 'accelerating' signal relies on a Q4FY26 revenue row (₹147 cr) that doesn't fit the FY26 total, and H1 PAT includes a one-off ₹81 cr gain from the AMC stake sale. Valuation is expensive: trailing P/E is 59.2x against a broad-market median of 35.2x (P77) and P/B is 12.8x (P90), well above what a 28.7% ROE supports. The 32x forward P/E needs roughly 80% earnings growth, yet sell-side FY-EPS estimates were cut 5.4% in the last 30 days. Earnings are not converting to cash: H1 operating cash flow was -₹828 cr as the loan book grew 51% to ₹5,294 cr, debt/equity is 3.0x, and this is a high-beta stock in a RISK_OFF regime with heavy FII selling.

Bandhan Bank is a mid-sized private bank that grew out of microfinance and is moving toward secured retail and wholesale lending: its retail book grew 42% YoY and wholesale 32%, while the legacy EEB (microfinance) book grew only 2%. In H1 FY27 PAT rose 132% YoY to Rs 1,123 cr on total income of Rs 7,190 cr (+9.0% YoY). That implies roughly Rs 621 cr PAT in Q2 against Rs 502 cr in Q1. The recovery is driven by credit costs, not core earnings: credit cost fell from 2.84% in FY26 to 0.44% in Q1, GNPA improved to 3.1% and NNPA to 0.9%, and PCR rose to 86.7%. Meanwhile operating profit fell 2% YoY (Rs 2,915 cr vs Rs 2,979 cr), even though NIM held at 6.2%. For a lender the right yardstick is price-to-book against ROE, not the 28.2x trailing P/E. At 1.35x P/B the stock is cheap against the broad market (P9 on P/B, P8 on forward P/E), but ROE is only 4.9% TTM and about 8.5% annualised for H1, below the 12% hurdle. On that basis I grade it fair, not cheap. The price sits at 95% of its 52-week range, so much of the asset-quality turnaround looks priced in. The biggest risk is funding: deposits grew 9% against 13% for advances, and the CASA ratio slipped from 29.4% to 27%, which could squeeze margins and limit growth.

fundamental.thesis: HUDCO is a government-owned infrastructure and housing development finance corporation (DFI) with a ₹1,73,123 cr loan book (28.8% YoY growth in Q1FY27), underpinned by implicit sovereign support and best-in-class asset quality (GNPA 1.08% declining from 1.21%, NNPA 0.06%, PCR 94.7%). Revenue growth has held firm at 28–31% across reported periods (H1FY26 +30.8% YoY), but PAT margin has compressed sharply from the ~30% FY26 full-year print (which carries a DATA_SUSPECT flag from a Q4 mismatch) to a cleaner ~21.2–21.6% at 9MFY26/H1FY26 — NIM has also slipped from 2.98% to 2.92%, signalling mild spread pressure as the rate cycle turns. Using the correct P/B+ROE yardstick for a lender (per sector card, not P/E): P/B of 2.35× against ROE of 20.2% represents clear undervaluation — the Dupont relationship implies an implied cost of equity ~8.6%, well below India's market rate — and peer rank confirms cheapness (P24 on P/B, P7 on P/E in a 473-stock universe), though the deeply negative CFO/PAT (−14× in H1FY26) and high structural leverage (D/E 645.77×) are significant watchpoints for cash-flow quality. The central risk is any slowdown in central or state government capex on housing and urban-infra schemes, which drives virtually all of HUDCO's origination and leaves it more exposed to policy-cycle risk than a diversified lender.

Revenue growth has decelerated from +23.5% (Q3FY26) to +16.9% (H1FY27, ₹3,238 cr) while PAT growth slowed to +14.3% YoY (₹1,854 cr); PAT margin at 57.2% in H1FY27 has compressed from the 60–61% range seen earlier, and EBITDA margins are on a contracting trajectory — the direction of change is negative even if absolute levels remain high. Using the sector-card mandated P/AUM-linked earnings yardstick, the stock trades at 51.33× trailing P/E and 35.11× EV/EBITDA (P74 vs broad market peers, +50% premium to median), with forward P/E of 36.77× implying priced-in earnings recovery — graded fair given the ROE-justified premium, but the stock at 83% of its 52-week range with consistently negative estimate revisions (FY-EPS cut –5.8% in 30d, next-FY cut –10.5% in 90d) provides very limited margin of safety. The biggest risk is a classic pre-derating setup: sell-side estimates being quietly cut while ratings remain bullish and the pending PMS acquisition from ICICI Securities adds regulatory and integration overhang.

Jammu & Kashmir Bank is a mid-sized regional lender that dominates its home state and is growing its retail, agriculture and MSME (RAM) book, with gross advances up 23.7% YoY to Rs 1.34 lakh Cr. In Q2FY27 net profit rose 10.6% YoY to Rs 546 Cr and reported income rose 14.7% YoY to Rs 1,817 Cr. Much of that came from other income, which doubled to Rs 315 Cr. Core net interest income grew only 5% YoY, and NIM has slipped from 3.64% to 3.28% over the trend window, while asset quality kept improving (gross NPA fell to 2.23% from 3.32%, net NPA to 0.51%, PCR 91.8%). Using the bank yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock looks cheap at 0.97x book for a 14.6% ROE (trailing P/E 6.97x, forward 5.76x), though the peer comparison is only against the broad market and earnings estimates have been cut 6.2% over the last 30 days. The biggest risk is funding: deposits are growing 16.3% against loans at 23.7%, and CASA has fallen from 45.9% to 42.0%, which could keep squeezing margins. ROA has also eased to 1.07%, and RBI penalties of Rs 68.65 Cr so far this year add a governance and operations flag.

fundamental.thesis: L&T Finance is a large retail-focused NBFC (₹1.32 lakh crore loan book) under the L&T Group umbrella, operating across rural/farm finance, two-wheelers, housing, and consumer lending segments with strong parentage and a well-capitalised balance sheet (CAR 18.67%). Revenue growth has sharply accelerated from +10.1% in H1FY26 to +24.4% in H1FY27, with PAT rising +31.6% YoY to ₹1,889 cr and PAT margins expanding from 16.5% to 17.6%; critically, the primary NBFC KPIs are moving in the right direction — Gross NPA has improved consistently from 3.19% to 2.75% over four periods, Net NPA from 0.96% to 0.85%, and ROA has risen to 2.39% from 2.27% in FY26, confirming this is not just revenue-led growth. Using P/B+ROE as the mandated NBFC yardstick (not P/E), LTF at 2.76× P/B with rising ROA ranks at P30 vs broad-market peers on both P/E and P/B (below sector median by 30–40%), and its trailing P/E of 24.57× sits within the 18–28× NBFC benchmark range while a forward P/E of 15.83× — a 36% discount to trailing — prices in strong near-term earnings growth, placing it at fair value with a modest cheap lean. The primary risk is that impairment provisions grew 15.6% YoY and credit cost remained elevated at 11.29% of total income, sell-side next-FY EPS estimates have been trimmed -3.2% over 30 days, and the highly leveraged balance sheet (D/E 393×) leaves LTF exposed to any funding-market stress or a slower-than-expected credit cost normalisation.

KFin Technologies is one of India's two main registrar and transfer agents, an asset-light fee business that grows with mutual fund AUM, folio counts, issuer services and international fund administration. I used Q1 FY27 because the Q2 FY27 results filed on 26-Oct have not been extracted yet. In Q1 FY27 revenue was ₹357 cr, up 30.1% YoY and faster than the +12–15% seen in Q1–Q2 FY26, but PAT was ₹75 cr, down 2.6% YoY. The PAT margin has fallen from 28–30% to 21.1%, so the extra revenue is not reaching profit, possibly because of acquisitions or costs. As a capital-markets fee business it does not suit the P/B-versus-ROE test used for lenders, so I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 45.2x and forward P/E 32.2x, about 28% above the broad-market median (P66), with EV/EBITDA at 27.3x (P60). That is fair rather than cheap for a business with 22% ROE, and the stock sits near the bottom fifth of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that revenue tracks the equity market: in a risk-off tape with only 10% of stocks above their 50-DMA, slowing AUM and flows could squeeze margins further. The press release headline claims margin expansion in Q2, but the official numbers have not been checked.

fundamental.thesis: Niva Bupa is a standalone health insurer with 11.1% of the retail health market, 26 million lives covered and retail health premiums up 47% YoY, so it is one of the fastest-growing players in an under-insured market. In Q1FY27, gross written premium rose 32.0% YoY to ₹2,150 cr and PAT rose 93% to ₹138 cr (6.4% margin, up from a loss of ₹9 cr in Q3FY26 and 2.1% for FY26). But the trend table mixes periods and bases (Q3FY26 revenue of ₹223 cr doesn't fit the other rows), and the combined ratio is 100.2%, so underwriting only breaks even and profit depends on investment income. A trailing P/E of 75× isn't meaningful for a business whose earnings are still ramping. On my yardstick for an insurer, P/B against ROE, 3.84× book for a 12.1% ROE is full, while the 23.5× forward P/E sits at the peer median (P51) and EV/EBITDA at P54, so I grade it fair: growth is priced in, not mispriced. The biggest risk is claims inflation pushing the combined ratio above 100%, with Q2FY27 results due within days; the 17-Oct exit of non-executive director Roger Davis is a minor governance item to watch.

Nippon Life India AMC is a top-5 Indian mutual fund manager with ₹7.87 trillion of MF quarterly average AUM, up 20% YoY. Its market share rose 51bps to 9.02%, led by ETFs (+135bps share gain) and B30 cities. Q2 FY27 revenue, derived as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹796 cr, up 21% YoY from ₹658 cr. That is in line with the +20% to +26% range of recent quarters. Reported Q2 PAT fell about 6% YoY to roughly ₹324 cr (40.7% margin), mainly because of a one-off ₹96.76 cr SEBI settlement over the AT-1 bonds, booked as an exceptional item. Excluding it, H1 operating profit of ₹1,211 cr (77.5% operating margin) shows the core business is healthy. Two weaker signs: closing AUM growth has slowed from +27% to +14% YoY over six periods, and SIP flows grew only 4% YoY. For an AMC the right yardstick is AUM-linked earnings, not P/B. Market cap is about 8.6% of the ₹8.68 trillion closing AUM, with a trailing P/E of 49x and forward P/E of 35x. That is fair for a franchise compounding above 20% with a 34.5% ROE. Upside is limited, though: the stock is at 99% of its 52-week range and sell-side FY EPS estimates were cut about 5% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that AMC earnings move with equity markets. In a risk-off market with heavy FII selling, falling equity AUM and slowing SIP growth could hit revenue quickly while the stock is priced near its highs.

fundamental.thesis: Home First Finance is a mid-sized affordable-housing lender that makes small-ticket home loans to salaried and self-employed borrowers. Its loan book is now about ₹14,900 cr, up 13.6% in the six months since March 2026. (The pack's '₹1,49,191 Cr' is almost certainly in ₹ millions, since the market cap is only ₹11,972 cr.) H1FY27 revenue rose 18.8% YoY to ₹1,105 cr and PAT rose 31.6% to ₹330 cr. That puts Q2FY27 at roughly ₹565 cr revenue (+19% YoY) and ₹170 cr PAT (+29%), so profit is still growing well but revenue growth has slowed from +31% in H1FY26 to about +19%, even though PAT margin improved from 26.9% to 29.8%. Lenders are judged on price-to-book against return on equity: at 2.74x book with a 15.7% ROE, a 22.2x trailing P/E (inside the 18–28x NBFC band) and a 14.9x forward P/E, the stock looks fair, not cheap, and sits at 40% of its 52-week range. The biggest gap is asset quality: gross NPA is 1.74% and net NPA 1.34% with only 23.6% provision coverage, and there is no H1FY27 data on interest margin or bad-loan trends to show whether credit quality is steady or slipping as the book grows fast.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Overseas Bank is a mid-sized public sector bank (market cap about ₹63,300 cr) that has recovered from its earlier bad-loan problems and now lends fast, with FY26 loan growth of 24.2%, a CASA (low-cost current and savings deposit) ratio of 41.0% and a FY26 NIM of 3.35%. In the latest quarter with filed numbers (Q1FY27), total income was ₹10,938 cr (+23.3% YoY) and profit after tax was ₹1,716 cr (+45.7% YoY), a 15.7% PAT margin. Asset quality also improved: gross NPA fell from 1.83% (H1FY26) to 1.42% (FY26), net NPA is 0.21%, provision coverage is about 97.5% and the capital ratio (CAR) is 19.8%. The 'accelerating/expanding' trajectory signals compare quarters against half-years and full years, so they can't be read as a clean trend, and the H1FY27 extract has no numbers. Valuation is graded on price-to-book against return on equity, the right yardstick for a bank: P/B of 1.63x on a 16.5% ROE sits just above the desk's 'cheap' line (P/B under 1.5x with ROE above 12%). That makes it fair, with a better entry because the stock is at 16% of its 52-week range, but it is not clearly mispriced for a PSU bank. The 36.5x forward P/E versus 11.0x trailing looks like a data error and I gave it no weight. The biggest risk is how durable earnings are. Much of the profit growth comes from very low credit costs (0.3% in FY26) and recoveries rather than core spread income. A 24% loan-growth pace in a risk-off market leaves less room for error, and the CFO change effective 01.11.2026 is a governance point to watch.

fundamental.thesis: Pine Labs is India's leading merchant commerce platform operating ~2.17 million POS/DCP devices with embedded affordability finance, UPI infrastructure, and an expanding international footprint (UAE, Malaysia) — a high-growth fintech rather than a traditional lender despite its Financials sector tag. Q1 FY27 revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹737 cr (stable within the 18-24% band across the last four quarters, showing consistent rather than truly accelerating growth), while PAT surged ~4× to ₹20 cr from ₹5 cr YoY, but EBITDA margin contracted sharply from 23% in Q3 FY26 to 17.1% in Q1 FY27 as technology/cloud spend (+33% YoY to ₹64 cr) and international investments eroded profitability — the trajectory signal of 'EBITDA contracting' is the dominant margin read. Valuation is expensive on most yardsticks: trailing P/E of 147× sits at P98 vs peers and far above any sector benchmark (IT 22–30×, Financials 12–18×); EV/EBITDA of 25.7× is more moderate at P58, and forward P/E of 31.7× (P67) is reasonable IF the earnings ramp materialises, but ROE of only 2.4% with D/E of 7.47 makes the P/B of 2.9× difficult to defend — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card's platform guidance, 'fair-to-expensive' is the honest grade, leaning expensive given the ROE/leverage combination. The biggest near-term risk is that the effective tax rate of 48% (vs guided 28-30%) and persistent EBITDA margin compression prevent the PAT inflection on which the forward multiple entirely depends, exposing the stock — already at its 52-week low — to further de-rating.

Five-Star Business Finance is a mid-sized NBFC that makes small secured business loans, backed by property, to self-employed borrowers in semi-urban and rural South India. It earns among the highest returns in the sector, with ROA around 7% and annualised ROE of 14.4% in H1 FY27. Growth has slowed sharply. Q2 FY27 total income was about ₹858 cr, up roughly 7.4% YoY from about ₹799 cr, and PAT was ₹299 cr, up roughly 4.7% from about ₹286 cr. Revenue growth over the trend window fell from +18% to +5–7%, and H1 PAT margin slipped 128 bps to 33.3%. For a lender I grade valuation on P/B against sustainable ROE rather than P/E. At 2.07x book with 16.1% TTM ROE, the stock sits between the cheap and expensive bands, so I call it fair. The 13.9x trailing P/E (10.6x forward) is below the 18–28x NBFC range and in the bottom quartile of the market, and estimate revisions are slightly positive. That discount looks deserved: the latest asset-quality figures I have (to 9M FY26) show gross NPA rising from 2.46% to 3.18% while provision coverage fell from 44.7% to 39%. The sector card treats rising bad loans with falling provisioning as a red flag that overrides other positives.

fundamental.thesis: Piramal Finance is a diversified mid-sized NBFC lending mainly to retail customers (housing, LAP, business and consumer loans). It is still running down a legacy wholesale and DHFL-inherited book, and has recently raised capital through a ₹2,100 cr QIP and ₹1,750 cr of promoter warrants. Q2 FY27, worked out as H1 minus Q1, shows revenue of about ₹3,585 cr, up roughly 27% YoY, and PAT of ₹545 cr, up 67% YoY. Revenue growth has stayed steady at about 27–28% for the last three periods, PAT margin rose from 11.6% in FY26 to about 15.2% this quarter, and gross NPA improved from 2.6% (Q3 FY26) to 2.26% (FY26). Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock is fair rather than cheap. P/B of 1.6x is cheap in absolute terms, but TTM ROE is only 5.4% (FY26 ROA 1.41%), and the 13.8x forward P/E (vs 30x trailing) already assumes earnings roughly double. With the stock at 89% of its 52-week range, a lot of the turnaround looks priced in. The biggest risk is that the legacy book and leverage (D/E about 2.75x, net debt about ₹82k cr) keep ROE from reaching the mid-teens. Sell-side EPS estimates have been trimmed 2–3% over the last 30–90 days even though 8 of 10 analysts rate it a buy, which is an early sign that expectations are running ahead of delivery.

fundamental.thesis: RBL Bank is a mid-size private sector lender undergoing a transformative reset — the recently RBI-approved amalgamation of Emirates NBD's Indian branches has materially scaled the balance sheet (advances +42% YoY to ₹1,42,314 cr) while an in-progress asset-quality clean-up has reduced GNPA from 2.78% six quarters ago to 1.02% today, the strongest trajectory signal in this pack. Q2FY27 delivered a step-change: net total income grew +29% YoY to ₹3,208 cr (NII component +37% at ₹2,131 cr, NIM expanding to 4.61%) and PAT surged +170% YoY to ₹482 cr (PAT margin: 15.0%), accelerating sharply from the +2.5%/+27% prints in Q1FY27 and reversing the -20% PAT decline seen in Q2FY26 — direction is unambiguously improving. Using P/B + ROE, the appropriate yardstick for lenders per the Sector Card: at P/B 1.36× the stock is optically below the cheap threshold, but ROE of 4.43% is mechanically depressed by an outsized CAR of 30.1% (2× typical regulatory minimums), making fair the more honest grade — the market has partially re-rated the name (stock at 96.2% of 52-week range) and at P33 on trailing P/E the consensus-peer view corroborates a fair assessment rather than a screaming-cheap one. The biggest risk is the sustained CASA ratio decline from 32.5% (Q1FY26) to 27.2% (Q2FY27), signalling a weakening liability franchise and rising cost of funds that could cap NIM improvement as the excess capital gets progressively deployed into the loan book.

PB Fintech runs PolicyBazaar and PaisaBazaar, India's largest online marketplaces for insurance and loans, with 28.1 Mn transacting customers. It earns fees on insurance and loans sold; it does not lend. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue grew 40.0% YoY to ₹1,888 cr and PAT grew 92% to ₹163 cr. PAT margin rose from about 6% to 8.6% YoY. Revenue growth is steady to slightly faster (+37% in Q3 FY26, +36.5% for FY26, +40% now). The pre-computed 'contracting margin' signal compares a seasonally weak Q1 with Q3 and the full year, so I don't read it as real deterioration. The New Initiatives segment still lost ₹36 cr at the Adjusted EBITDA level. This is a platform business, so I graded valuation on price-to-sales, growth and unit economics rather than the lender P/B+ROE test. On that basis it is expensive. Price/sales is 11.0×, trailing P/E is 111× and forward P/E is 47.8×, against a broad-market median of 23.2×. EV/EBITDA is 140.6× (P99 vs peers). Even 40% growth does not fully justify these multiples. The biggest near-term risk is the Q2 FY27 results due 30-Oct-2026. Sell-side estimates for next year have been cut 6.8% over 90 days, and at these multiples any slowdown in protection premiums or delay in New Initiatives breakeven would be punished hard.

fundamental.thesis: Sammaan Capital is a restructuring NBFC/housing-finance company that completed a major business-model transformation in FY26 — reclassifying ₹14,953 cr of non-core exposures to hold-to-sell (crystallising a ₹6,499 cr exceptional loss) — while Abu Dhabi-based IHC stepped in as a ₹8,850 cr strategic investor and now controls the company as promoter. Q1FY27 revenue fell 30.1% YoY to ₹1,683 cr (from ₹2,409 cr), driven by a near-total collapse in derecognition gains (₹732 cr → ₹24 cr) and declining interest income, with PAT of ₹243 cr (-27.2% YoY) at a 14.5% margin — the operating business remains marginally profitable, but the loan book is actively shrinking (-19.79% in FY26), structurally compressing the income base. Valuation is assessed on P/B + ROE as mandated for lenders: P/B at 0.75x is optically cheap (P1 in broad market, cheapest cohort), but ROE TTM is -35% (distorted by FY26 exceptional items), which disqualifies the standard 'cheap' threshold (P/B < 1.5 + ROE > 12%); on a normalised run-rate of ~₹1,000 cr PAT annualised from Q1FY27, forward P/E approximates 20x — within the NBFC 18–28x range — making this speculative 'fair' contingent on loan-book stabilisation. The largest risk is structural: finance costs consume 79.3% of total income against D/E of 273x, so any further top-line compression from the shrinking book or credit-cost normalisation quickly erodes the thin 14% operating margin, notwithstanding the current 20.06% CAR cushion.

SBFC Finance is a mid-sized NBFC (Middle Layer under RBI rules) that lends secured MSME and gold loans. Its gross loan book is ₹11,161 cr, up 13.8% since FY26 year-end, and FY26 return on assets was 4.6%. In H1 FY27, revenue grew 29.9% YoY to ₹1,038 cr and PAT grew 28.1% to ₹269 cr. Growth has stayed in a steady 28–31% band for the last five periods, with only a slight deceleration. PAT margin dipped from 26.3% to 25.9%, and asset quality held steady to slightly better: GNPA was 2.64% against 2.77% a year ago, and NNPA 1.54% against 1.51%. On valuation I used the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, not P/E. At 2.71x book with a 13% ROE, the stock is fair: well above the cheap zone for a 13% ROE, but justified by around 30% book growth. The 22.4x trailing P/E sits in the NBFC 18–28x band, the 18.4x forward P/E is below trailing, and analysts raised EPS estimates by about 2.5% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that growth is being bought by weakening the balance sheet. Provision coverage fell from 46.2% to 42.2%, capital adequacy fell from 34.1% to 31.3%, and debt-to-equity rose from 1.80 to 2.31. If credit costs normalise in a risk-off, rupee-weak macro, earnings could compress quickly for a midcap lender.

fundamental.thesis: UCO Bank is a mid-sized public sector bank with ₹6.37 lakh crore of total business and a mostly retail, agriculture and MSME loan book (₹1.69 lakh crore of ₹2.88 lakh crore gross advances). Loan growth has sped up from 16.6% to 25.2% over five periods, and asset quality keeps improving: gross NPA fell from 2.56% to 1.96%, net NPA from 0.43% to 0.18%, and provision coverage is 98.4%. For a lender I grade value on price-to-book against return on equity, as the sector card says, rather than P/E. The 12.7x trailing P/E is irrelevant for a bank. Forward P/E is 20.0x, above the trailing figure, which points to lower expected earnings. The biggest risk is funding: loans grew 24.7% but CASA deposits grew only 10.6%, the CASA ratio slipped from 38.65% to 36.77%, and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%, so growth is leaning on costlier deposits and could squeeze the 3.0% NIM.

fundamental.thesis: Union Bank of India is a large public-sector lender, and its asset quality and loan growth are clearly getting better. In Q2 FY27, total income rose only +3.2% YoY to ₹32,809 cr, but PAT jumped +29.9% to ₹5,537 cr, pushing the PAT margin up to 16.9% from 13.4% a year ago. Under the hood the trend is clean: NIM rose from 2.67% to 2.86% over four quarters, gross NPA fell from 3.29% to 2.42%, net NPA fell to 0.42%, credit cost is low at 0.21%, and loan growth sped up from about 5% to about 13% YoY. Using the P/B-plus-ROE yardstick for lenders (P/E is ignored for banks), the stock trades at 1.01× book against a 15.7% TTM ROE (17.2% in Q2), so it is cheap. That reading is backed by a bottom-3rd-percentile rank on P/B. The main caution is that profits are rising much faster than income, which leans on low provisions and margin gains that may not last as rates reset, and 164 fraud cases (₹1,206 cr, nearly all already provided for) are a reminder of PSU governance and underwriting risk.

UTI AMC is one of India's older mid-sized mutual fund houses, with pension, alternatives and international businesses on top. Its earnings move with equity AUM and flows. Revenue for H1FY27 was ₹983 cr, up only 1.8% YoY, while PAT grew 10.4% to ₹426 cr. Q2FY27 alone, worked out as H1 minus Q1, looks weaker: revenue of about ₹399 cr fell roughly 4-5% YoY and slowed from +6.7% in Q1. PAT of about ₹132 cr was up sharply from a weak base, a 33% margin, but down from 50% in Q1, and cash conversion was only 0.60x CFO/PAT. The card's yardstick for AMCs is price against AUM-linked earnings, but no AUM or flow data was provided, so I used P/E as a proxy: trailing 30.5x is about 13% below the broad-market median of 35x (P42). The forward P/E of 16.7x and the 2.8x P/B with 9.8% ROE look distorted by one-off items in the trailing base, so I grade valuation fair rather than cheap, even with the stock near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is in a risk-off market: flat fee income, the international segment down 27.5%, and a 120% dividend payout leave little room if equity AUM and flows weaken.

fundamental.thesis: Cyient is a mid-cap engineering services firm. Its core DET segment is about 74% of revenue and the rest comes from electronics manufacturing (DLM) and a young semiconductor business, so it is more than a pure IT-services name. H1 FY27 revenue grew 23.4% YoY to ₹4,311 cr, but much of that came from acquisitions such as TAO Digital and the semiconductor build-out. PAT fell 19.7% YoY to ₹241 cr, cutting the PAT margin from 8.6% to 5.6%. The semiconductor segment runs at a -16.5% margin and the trend table shows EBITDA margin sliding from 14.5% to 13.0%, so profits are not keeping up with sales. On valuation, I used the IT P/E benchmark, cross-checked with EV/EBITDA because of the mix of services and manufacturing. A trailing P/E of 22.6x sits at the bottom of the IT range of 22–30x, and EV/EBITDA of 11.4x is about half the market median. That looks optically cheap, but ROE is only 7.8%. The 11.9x forward P/E assumes a sharp earnings rebound while sell-side estimates were cut 18% over 90 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the debt-funded semiconductor push and the goodwill-heavy TAO deal (₹1,724 cr of goodwill) keep eating into profits. The stock trades at 20% of its 52-week range, which suggests the market is already discounting some of this.

fundamental.thesis: One 97 Communications (Paytm) is a leading Indian digital payments and merchant platform that also distributes loans and financial services. It is now consistently profitable and has a strong net cash position of ₹12,714 cr. From the filings, Q2FY27 revenue is about ₹2,648 cr (H1 ₹5,096 cr minus Q1 ₹2,448 cr), up roughly 28.5% YoY from ₹2,061 cr, and PAT is about ₹225 cr against ₹21 cr a year ago. Revenue growth has picked up from +22% in FY26 to +28%, and the PAT margin has risen from 1.0% to about 8.5% over the trend window, though PAT was only flat quarter-on-quarter (₹220 cr to ₹225 cr). This is a newly profitable platform, so P/E is not the right yardstick. Judged on EV/sales against growth and margin trajectory, the stock still looks expensive: price/sales is 8.3x, EV/EBITDA is 112.8x (P98 vs the broad market) and ROE is only 3.6% at 4.4x book. The forward P/E of 34.9x already assumes earnings roughly triple, so upside depends heavily on the MDR (a fee merchants pay on each payment), which management says will be introduced after Diwali 2026 on a date not yet notified. The biggest risk is regulatory: the MDR date, the ₹611 cr FEMA show-cause notice and the ₹704 cr GST demand on its gaming joint venture are all unresolved, in a risk-off market that is negative for Financials.

fundamental.thesis: MRPL is a PSU mid-cap refinery (ONGC subsidiary) processing ~4.4 MMT/quarter of crude at Mangalore, operating in a policy-administered margin environment where GRMs, not crude price alone, drive earnings. H1FY27 revenue surged +67.6% YoY to ₹77,199 cr and PAT exploded +697.6% YoY to ₹2,846 cr (PAT margin 3.7%), a dramatic recovery from the near-zero-profit FY26 base (PAT margin 1.8%), with EBITDA margin expanding to 6.6% on strong throughput and higher product realisations — though a fire incident at the CHT unit on 30-Sep-2026 provisionally cost ₹118 cr and creates near-term operational uncertainty. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive refinery (per sector card guidance for PSU OMCs/refiners), MRPL trades at 5.97× EV/EBITDA versus a broad-market median of 23.3× — placing it at P3 in its peer universe — making it structurally cheap, though the sector card explicitly cautions this discount is 'policy-priced' (permanent policy risk, not a valuation error); trailing P/E of 14.5× sits at the upper end of the PSU OMC range (6–10× + yield), but the forward P/E collapses to 3.4×, implying the street is pricing in a very strong FY27 full-year earnings recovery. The key risk is that elevated crude at $97.97/bbl directly compresses refining marketing margins for OMC-adjacent refiners, estimate revisions are sharply negative (-9.6% 30d, -21.2% next-FY 90d) signalling analyst concern about GRM sustainability, and the CHT fire adds operational/insurance settlement uncertainty over the next 1–2 quarters.

fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue grew +12.8% YoY to ₹1,075 cr — a clear acceleration from +5.4% in Q1FY26 — with PAT rising faster at +22.9% to ₹395 cr and PAT margin expanding to 36.7% from 25.3%; the EBITDA margin, however, contracted to 54.7% from 62.5% quarter-on-quarter, the residential segment effectively shut down at -92% YoY, and FY26 full-year CFO/PAT of 0.34× signals that a large portion of reported earnings is not yet converting to operating cash. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

TTML is Tata's small enterprise-focused wireline and data business in Maharashtra, a niche player rather than one of the mobile oligopoly companies that benefit from tariff hikes. Revenue has turned around: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹611 cr, up 7.2% YoY from ₹570 cr, after falling 11–15% YoY across FY26. The net loss narrowed to ₹131 cr in H1 FY27 from ₹646 cr a year earlier, and quarterly losses improved from ₹72 cr in Q1 to ₹59 cr in Q2. PAT margin was still about -21.5%, and one quarter of growth after five periods of decline is not yet a confirmed trend. P/E and P/B mean nothing here: the company is loss-making (the 187x trailing P/E is a data artefact) and net worth is negative at about -₹19,983 cr. So I used EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick. At 47x it is about 4x the 9–12x telecom norm and at the P87 level of the broad market, so the stock is expensive even though it trades near its 52-week low (15% of range). The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt service coverage is only 0.10x and interest coverage 1.09x, so the company depends on continued Tata Group support to refinance or service its debt.

Per the sector card, P/E (55.2×) is structurally meaningless for developers; using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick, PRESTIGE trades at 21.6× — a 7.2% discount to the broad-market peer median of 23.3× (P46), placing it as fairly valued on the sector-appropriate metric; P/B of 4.0× with an ROE of only 8.0% is unimpressive in isolation but undervalues the embedded land bank and unrecognised backlog. The critical single risk is extreme financial leverage (D/E 105×) in a RISK_OFF macro regime with rising crude ($90.41, a direct construction-cost headwind) and a US 10Y yield at 5.29%, which together could compress developer spreads and raise refinancing costs if pre-sales momentum or collections slow.

HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, and its liability franchise is growing fast: deposits are up 18.8% YoY and advances up 16.3% YoY, and asset quality is very clean (GNPA 1.11%, NNPA 0.37%, credit cost 44 bps, CAR 18.9%). The earnings picture has weakened, though. H1FY27 revenue of ₹251,616 cr fell 4.1% YoY and PAT of ₹35,869 cr fell 10.2% YoY, after growing about 11% and 10% in FY26. NIM is at a cycle low of 3.32%, and the CASA ratio has slipped to 31.6%, which keeps funding costs high. Management says margins bottomed in Q2 and should rise from Q3, because the October 25 bp rate hike reprices the 70%-floating loan book. On the lender yardstick (P/B against ROE), 1.98x book for a 12–14% ROE is fair: above the 1.5x level we would call cheap, well below the 3x level that would be expensive, and P79 on P/B among regional bank peers. The stock sits near its 52-week low and forward P/E is 12.0x against trailing 16.8x, but FY EPS estimates were cut 5.6% over 30 days even though 40 of 42 analysts rate it a buy, so the near-term re-rating case is weak. The main risks are leadership and the balance sheet: the MD & CEO change took effect immediately and the Deputy MD retires in December, while the loan-to-deposit ratio is about 100% and LCR is 113%, near the bottom of its target range.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance Industries is India's largest private-sector conglomerate, spanning oil-to-chemicals refining, Jio telecom, retail and new energy, so it should be valued as four businesses rather than as an oil company. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue rose 24.5% YoY to ₹340,257 cr, but PAT rose only 6.1% to ₹23,196 cr, and margins are shrinking: PAT margin fell from about 8.1–8.3% in FY26 to 6.8%, and EBITDA margin fell from 17.7% to 15.9%. Sales are growing much faster than profits, although cash conversion stays strong (FY26 CFO/PAT 2.2x, FCF ₹38,736 cr). The sector card says to value RELIANCE as a sum of its parts, but no sum-of-the-parts inputs were provided, so I used EV/EBITDA as the yardstick. At 12.2x EV/EBITDA and 21.7x trailing P/E, the stock looks expensive against its PSU energy peers (median 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x P/E). Those peers carry permanent policy risk and are not a fair comparison for a conglomerate with telecom and retail arms, so I grade valuation as fair, with a forward P/E of 18.0x and the price near its 52-week low as mild supports. The biggest near-term uncertainty is tomorrow's Q2FY27 result (board meeting on 30 Oct), the first after Jio Platforms listed on 28 Oct at a ₹1,119 issue price; together with the shrinking margins and crude above $100, it could move both earnings and how the market values the group.

fundamental.thesis: Bharti Airtel is the number-two player in India's three-player mobile market, which has stopped competing on price, with Africa, enterprise, home broadband and data-centre businesses on top. fundamental.thesis: Tata Capital is the Tata group's diversified NBFC, with a ₹3.08L cr AUM that is 85% retail/SME across 1,515 branches, plus a housing-finance arm (TCHFL, ₹95k cr AUM, 18% ROE). Asset quality also improved: credit cost fell from 1.3% to 0.9%, gross Stage-3 is 1.9%, net Stage-3 is 0.8%, ROA rose from 1.9% to 2.3%, ROE from 13% to 14%, and cost-to-income fell from 39.7% to 35.3%. The pre-computed 'decelerating revenue / contracting margin' signals mix gross-income and net-income periods and should be ignored, since the KPIs show a clearly improving trend. Using the P/B-versus-ROE yardstick for lenders, a P/B of 3.83x for a 12–14% ROE is rich, and trailing P/E of 29.4x is above the 18–28x NBFC range. The 16.6x forward P/E and AUM growth of 26% partly justify this, so the grade is expensive rather than egregious. The biggest risk is capital: the capital adequacy ratio (CRAR) has fallen from 20.3% to 17.3% within three quarters while AUM grows 26% and the Yogakshemam gold-loan acquisition is still pending, so growth may soon need fresh equity at 5.5x debt-to-equity in a risk-off funding market.

fundamental.thesis: Infosys is India's second-largest IT services exporter, a debt-free, cash-generative tier-1 franchise now caught in the sector's AI reset, where productivity gains are shrinking legacy time-and-materials revenue. H1FY27 revenue was ₹97,454 cr, up only +1.9% YoY (Q2 constant-currency growth +1.5%, down from +2.4% in Q1 and +3.1% for FY26). H1 PAT was ₹15,613 cr, up +9.2%, but PAT margin slipped from 16.5% to 16.0%, and the FY27 revenue guide was cut to 1–2% cc from 1.5–3.5% even though the trend table labels it 'maintained'. Using trailing P/E as the yardstick for an asset-light IT services firm, 15.8× sits well below the 22–30× sector range and 36% below the peer median of 24.7× (P12), so the stock grades cheap, at about 10–18% of its 52-week range. The offsets are $5.2B of H1 large-deal TCV (62% net new), AI revenue at 10.5% of total and FCF at about 113% of PAT. The biggest risk is that the discount is a value trap: shrinking legacy revenue, a guidance cut and small but steady estimate cuts (-0.3% over 30 days) may mean the low multiple reflects a lasting slowdown rather than a mispricing.

Delhivery is one of India's largest tech-led third-party logistics companies, covering express parcel, part-truckload and supply-chain services, and it bought Ecom Express in 2025 to gain scale. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 27.8% YoY to ₹2,931 cr, up from about 16-17% in FY26, but much of that jump comes from the Ecom acquisition. PAT fell 65% YoY to ₹32 cr, the PAT margin dropped from about 4.0% to 1.1%, and EBITDA fell 6.6% YoY to ₹253 cr even though revenue rose. The pre-computed signal that EBITDA margin is 'expanding' conflicts with these filing figures, and Q2/Q3 FY26 data is missing. This is a thin-margin, still-scaling logistics platform rather than an order-book capital-goods business, so I graded it on EV/EBITDA and EV/sales instead of P/E. On that basis it is expensive: EV/EBITDA is 111x, near the top of the broad market (P98, against a median of 23x), and trailing P/E is 231x. Forward P/E of 41x is still above the market median of 23x, ROE is only 1.6%, and the stock sits at 79% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the Q2FY27 results on 30 Oct: analysts have already cut FY EPS estimates by 13% over 90 days, and another quarter of falling margins from Ecom integration costs would undercut the profitability story that today's price already assumes.

Using EV/EBITDA (24.4×) as the primary yardstick for capital-intensive specialty chemicals (per sector card), the stock sits at P56 versus broad market peers — fairly valued — with trailing P/E at 38.77× well above the 12–22× Materials sector benchmark, partially justified by franchise-quality margins; however, 90-day sell-side EPS revisions of -4.5% directly undermine the steep earnings recovery that the 26× forward P/E implies. The biggest risk is that the combination of negative revenue growth (-2.2%), contracting PAT margins, and extremely weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT of only 0.32× in HY FY26) could derate this premium multiple materially if the Q2FY27 results confirm operational deterioration rather than a cyclical bottom.

fundamental.thesis: Blue Jet Healthcare is a specialty pharmaceutical-intermediates and contrast-media (iohexol, saccharin) company, best framed as a CDMO-adjacent franchise with lumpy quarterly demand tied to a narrow product slate. Revenue growth decelerated sharply from +117.8% in Q1FY26 to +8.7% for full-year FY26, while PAT fell -18.8% YoY and PAT margins compressed from 29.6% (FY25) to 24.1% (FY26), confirming both a high-base headwind and real operating-cost pressures rather than a one-quarter blip. At a trailing P/E of 42.55× (above the 28–40× pharma sector upper bound) and EV/EBITDA of 35.84× (at the P75 expensive peer threshold), the stock carries an unjustified premium during a period of earnings decline — forward P/E of 29.51× prices in sharp recovery that has not yet appeared in official filings. The QIP allotment of ~1.58 cr shares at ₹506 (post-quarter) dilutes the share count by roughly 9% at a discount to market, and the reported debt/equity of 3.1 adds balance-sheet fragility, making per-share earnings recovery materially harder to achieve.

Nuvoco Vistas is an East- and North-focused cement and ready-mix concrete (RMC) maker with about 35 MTPA of target capacity. It is a mid-tier player in a sector where UltraTech and Adani now control about 45% of capacity. Using the filings trend table (the yfinance rows are inconsistent and were ignored), Q2FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹2,790 cr, up from +9.0% in Q1, and cement volumes grew 9% YoY against 5% in Q1. Profit quality is thinner than the headline suggests. PAT rose 78% YoY, but only to ₹65 cr, a 2.3% margin. EBITDA margin fell to 14.7% from 18.3% in Q1 and 15.1% a year ago. Implied EBITDA per tonne is about ₹875, below the healthy ₹900–1,100 band and down from roughly ₹1,080 in Q1. Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cement maker, not P/E. At 8.6x (P8 of the broad market, no close peers in the universe), with P/B of 1.09x, forward P/E of 20.5x against trailing 31x, and the price at 18% of its 52-week range, the stock looks cheap against typical cement multiples. Much of that discount is justified by an ROE of only 3.7% and high debt. The biggest risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is ₹5,028 cr, current ratio is 0.57x, free cash flow was -₹246 cr in H1 because of capex, and legal disputes are pending: the ₹490 cr CCI penalty and about ₹454 cr of West Bengal incentive provisions. These come on top of rising crude and a weak rupee pushing up fuel and freight costs.

fundamental.thesis: NATCO Pharma is a mid-sized specialty generics maker whose profits have depended heavily on a few complex US launches, especially the gRevlimid windfall (FY25 US revenue was about ₹3,760 cr out of ₹4,430 cr total). Its growth is clearly shrinking: FY26 revenue fell 7.9% to ₹4,078 cr and PAT fell 24.8% to ₹1,418 cr, with PAT margin sliding from 42.6% to 34.8%. Q1 FY27 numbers did not extract, and the FY27 PAT guidance of about ₹750 cr points to profit roughly halving as the windfall runs off. The only bright spot is domestic formulations, which grew about 25%. I graded valuation on P/E after stripping out the one-off windfall income. The trailing P/E of 11.2× (P9 vs the broad market) looks cheap, but only because it still includes windfall profits. On guided FY27 earnings the stock trades at about 21× (forward P/E 19.3×, P36 vs the broad market). That is below the 28–40× pharma range but justified by falling earnings, so I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is what replaces gRevlimid: value now depends on unnamed US launches, a Carfilzomib launch not due until calendar 2027, and how well management spends the roughly ₹2,000 cr it raised (the rights issue is now allotted) on M&A that has not been announced.

fundamental.thesis: Meesho is India's largest social commerce marketplace targeting value-conscious consumers in tier 2–4 cities, with 274 million annual transacting users, 1.04 million active sellers, and dominant penetration in the unorganised mass-market ecommerce segment. Q1FY27 marketplace revenue grew 48% YoY to ₹3,707 crore with NMV expanding 34% YoY to ₹11,614 crore and contribution margin improving to 4.6% of NMV (+54bps QoQ), but adjusted EBITDA remains negative at -1.2% of NMV and LTM FCF burns ₹537 crore — growth is still being bought, not yet earned. Using EV/sales as the correct yardstick for a pre-profit platform (P/E is not meaningful here per sector card), P/S of 6.22× for a cash-burning EBITDA-negative business is unambiguously expensive — the stock sits at P99 across 472 broad-market peers on forward P/E (94.9× vs 23.2× median, +309% premium), offering zero margin of safety against any execution stumble. The D/E of 1.43 is a structural concern for a loss-making platform, an independent director resigned on 15 Oct, next-FY sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 21.2% over 90 days, and the RISK_OFF macro environment with rising crude provides twin headwinds to discretionary consumption and platform unit economics.

Poly Medicure is a medical-devices maker focused on infusion, vascular access and dialysis consumables, with a large export business and 19 overseas subsidiaries and associates; a weaker rupee and the China+1 shift help it. We cannot read the latest-quarter trend reliably because the extracted figures contradict each other: FY26 revenue shows as both ₹995 cr and ₹3,076 cr, PAT margin swings between 10.8% and 73.2%, and the yfinance Q1FY27 row has PAT of ₹86 cr on revenue of only ₹140 cr. We therefore make no growth or margin claim, and the Q1FY27 PDF numbers have not been indexed. We graded valuation on trailing P/E because the Healthcare card gives no devices-specific yardstick: at 49.6x it is above the 28–40x healthcare benchmark, which makes it expensive. Against the broad market it is about the 70th percentile on P/E and EV/EBITDA (33.8x), and P/B of 5.1x on 10.8% ROE is a rich price for that level of return. The forward P/E of 33.6x is only justified if earnings growth comes through, and the next test is the Q2FY27 results on 5 Nov 2026. The other risk is capital allocation: management is moving into an unrelated business, Himalayan Mineral Waters, bought through insolvency proceedings, while some overseas subsidiaries are posting losses.

fundamental.thesis: The Leela Palaces Hotels & Resorts is a pure-play luxury hotel owner-operator with 14 properties at Q3FY26 and an average room rate of about ₹30,300, which puts it squarely in the premium-travel trend the sector card calls structurally strong while hotel supply lags demand until about 2027. The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹352 cr, up 28.1% YoY, and PAT of ₹49 cr, up 460% off a low base, for a 13.8% PAT margin. Revenue growth sped up from +21.0% in Q3FY26. The trend table flags margins as 'contracting' (from 32.3%/52.0% EBITDA in Q3FY26), but that compares the seasonally weak Q1 against peak-season Q3, so it is not a real deterioration. The Q2/H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-14 have not been extracted, so the latest quarter is unverified. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hotel owner, the stock trades at 22.5×, about level with the 23.3× median (P48), and P/B is 2.4× against an ROE of only 8%. That makes it fair, not cheap, despite 18 of 18 analysts rating it buy and FY-EPS estimates raised 8.7% over 90 days. The main risks are a mid-cap luxury-discretionary stock in a RISK_OFF market with rising crude, and the live price data contradicting itself: the 52-week range of ₹382–474 conflicts with the consensus target of ₹702 implying +16.9% upside, and yfinance Q1 revenue of ₹114 cr does not match the PDF figure of ₹352 cr.

fundamental.thesis: Hyundai Motor India is India's second-largest passenger-vehicle maker, with an SUV-heavy mix, and it just opened a new plant in Pune (inaugurated 14-Oct-2026). Its latest reported quarter, Q1FY27, was weak: revenue was flat at ₹16,335 cr (-0.5% YoY) while PAT fell 35.1% YoY to ₹889 cr. EBITDA margin dropped about 370 bps to 10.9%, and the margin trend has fallen steadily from 15.0% to 12.6%, 12.2% and now 10.9%, so costs, a weaker mix or new-plant start-up costs are eating into profits rather than demand collapsing. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the measure for a capital-intensive business: 21.2x is slightly below the broad-market median (P45). But the trailing P/E of 36.2x is above the 18–30x auto OEM range, and the forward P/E of 23.8x only holds up if earnings recover sharply. Analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by 4.7% over 90 days while 24 of 28 still rate it a buy, so on balance I grade it expensive, not cheap. The biggest near-term test is Q2 results on 28-Oct-2026: they will show whether festive-season volumes and the Pune ramp-up can rebuild margins in a risk-off market with crude rising.

fundamental.thesis: BBTC is the Wadia Group's holding company with a controlling stake in Britannia Industries plus tea/coffee plantations and auto-electrical components — P/E comparison to pure FMCG operators is structurally misleading, and the correct yardstick here is P/B plus EV/EBITDA (sector card conglomerate guidance), not the 40–65× FMCG P/E benchmark. Using yfinance (Q1FY27 official PDF data is absent from the trend table), revenue grew +5.9% YoY to ₹2,959 cr, decelerating from +8.7% in Q1FY26, while PAT margin expanded sharply to ~9.7% (from 5.1% in Q1FY26) — though that expansion likely includes volatile Britannia dividend and investment income rather than structural operating improvement (note H1FY26 CFO/PAT was −0.02×, a poor cash-conversion signal for the operating businesses). On EV/EBITDA of 3.06× (P0 in broad market) and P/B of 1.42× with the stock at 14.6% of its 52-week range, BBTC appears deeply cheap by any metric — but a structural holding-company discount of 30–50% is normal and persistent, and the extreme D/E of 16.57 with US 10Y at 5.29% and rising is an offsetting overhang that explains why the discount exists. The biggest risk is that debt is likely collateralised against the Britannia stake, meaning a sustained FII-driven de-rating of Britannia under the current RISK_OFF regime could trigger a collateral squeeze at the BBTC level, amplifying downside disproportionately.

fundamental.thesis: Birlasoft is a mid-tier IT services firm focused on enterprise applications (ERP/CRM), with manufacturing as its largest vertical (39% of revenue); it sits on about ₹2,453 cr of net cash, and the recent OpenAI Select Partner tie-up has not yet shown up in revenue. Revenue has been flat to falling: FY26 consolidated revenue fell 1.2% YoY to ₹5,310 cr, Q3FY26 fell 1.1% (₹1,348 cr), and manufacturing shrank 5.7%. PAT was ₹518 cr (+0.3%), helped only by EBITDA margin rising to 16.8% from 15.0%, while operating cash flow fell 18%. These figures are stale: the latest official extraction is FY26, Q1FY27 has not been indexed, and the yfinance Q1FY27 row (₹840 cr revenue) does not reconcile with run-rate quarterly revenue of about ₹1,300 cr, so it is treated as suspect. On valuation, the stock looks cheap against the IT sector band of 22–30x, at 13.8x trailing P/E, 11.4x forward and 6.1x EV/EBITDA near its 52-week low (EV/EBITDA used as the main yardstick because cash distorts P/E). fundamental.thesis: BHEL is India's dominant PSU power equipment and heavy engineering manufacturer, with leading exposure to thermal power, defence, and T&D — a direct beneficiary of the government-led capex upcycle in power and infrastructure. Q2FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹9,300 cr (+23.8% YoY from ₹7,512 cr), PAT surged 118.9% to ₹821 cr (margin 8.8%), confirming a clear multi-period turnaround: PAT margins have expanded from -0.7% in H1FY26 through 4.5%, 4.7%, 4.9%, to 8.8% now, with H1FY27 PAT of ₹1,198 cr vs a ₹80.6 cr loss a year ago. On the primary Industrials yardstick (EV/EBITDA), BHEL trades at 56.2× vs sector median 34.0× — P88 in sector, a 65% premium — and while the forward P/E of 29.7× is a reassuring P35 (below median), the stock is at 82.6% of its 52-week range with ROE of only 6.3% against P/B of 5.15×, graded expensive overall. The most critical data gap is the absence of current order-book and book-to-bill figures, which are the primary leading indicator for any capital-goods name; without these, it is impossible to confirm that the execution ramp is sustainable, and any government capex pause could trigger the 30–50% de-rating this sector is historically prone to from near-highs.

Astral is a leading Indian maker of plastic pipes and fittings, with a growing adhesives arm. Its sales follow real-estate and building-materials demand rather than an infrastructure order book, so the Industrials sector card's order-book metrics don't really apply. The official filings data is messy and partly stale. The cleanest numbers, for 9MFY26, show revenue up 7.9% year on year to ₹4,480 cr while PAT fell 6.0% to ₹324 cr. Earnings growth was single-digit for revenue and negative for profit through FY26. The Q4FY26 and FY26 rows in the trend table look wrongly extracted, and Q1FY27 results are not in the filings index. yfinance shows Q1FY27 revenue of ₹938 cr and PAT of ₹120 cr, but those numbers are unverified. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, with peer rank and P/E as checks. EV/EBITDA is 35.7×, only 5% above the sector peer median of 34.0×. Trailing P/E is 68.2×, above the 28–45× sector benchmark, but only P62 among peers. Forward P/E of 43.3× implies a big earnings recovery is already expected, so I call it fair, leaning expensive. The biggest risk is that this recovery doesn't arrive. Crude above $100 raises PVC and polymer costs, and housing-linked demand is soft in a risk-off market. Either could squeeze margins again before Q2 results on 5 Nov.

Deepak Nitrite is India's largest maker of phenol, acetone, IPA and sodium nitrite, and it is spending heavily on integrated downstream specialty chemicals (₹2,500 cr capex planned for FY27). In Q1 FY27, revenue rose 36.4% YoY to ₹2,578 cr and PAT rose 207% to ₹345 cr, taking PAT margin to 13.4%, up from 5–7% through FY26 (FY26 revenue -4.8%, PAT -20.5%). Much of the jump comes from a weak prior-year base, it is only one strong quarter after a year of decline, and the Q2 FY27 results filed today have not been extracted yet, so the trend may already have moved. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for chemical cyclicals: at 24.6x it is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm and 37% above the Materials peer median of 17.9x (P67). Trailing P/E of 41.6x and P/B of 3.9x against a 9.8% ROE also point to expensive, so the valuation already assumes the new capacity ramps up smoothly. The biggest risk is the phenolics spread: if it reverses, or if China dumping pushes prices down, margins could slip back to FY26 levels while capex and depreciation keep rising.

fundamental.thesis: JM Financial is a mid-size diversified financial services group spanning Investment Banking, Wealth Management, Asset Management, Private Markets (ARC/distressed credit), and Affordable Home Loans, with a total AUM of ₹1,48,661 cr. Adani Energy Solutions is India's largest private power transmission company, with about 30% share of transmission awards. It also runs the Mumbai distribution business and a fast-growing smart-meter business, so most of its earnings come from regulated assets as they are built and commissioned. H1 FY27 revenue rose 47.5% YoY to ₹19,787 cr and PAT rose 137% to ₹2,600 cr. Working back from the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 revenue was about ₹10,076 cr (roughly +53% YoY) and PAT about ₹1,451 cr, a 14.4% margin. Growth sped up from +42.4% in Q1 and margins improved from 11.7%, helped by full-year HVDC Mumbai tariffs and higher distribution revenue. On the yardstick that fits a capital-intensive regulated utility (EV/EBITDA, plus P/B against ROE), the stock looks expensive: EV/EBITDA is 25.1x, P/B is 7.2x against only 9.7% ROE, and trailing P/E is 81.7x against a 10–18x utilities median. The price is also at 89.5% of its 52-week range, so the large forward capitalisation pipeline (₹21,000 cr planned for FY27) already looks largely priced in, even though analysts are raising estimates (+16% over 30 days). The biggest risk is the balance sheet: net debt is about ₹49,156 cr (6.2x EBITDA), capex of ₹9,442 cr in H1 was far above operating cash flow of ₹6,257 cr, and free cash flow was negative. That leaves the stock exposed to funding costs, Adani group news, and when regulators approve deferral-account items.

IEX runs India's dominant power exchange, a capital-light platform business with very high margins; it is tagged Financials, but it is not a lender, so the P/B+ROE yardstick for lenders does not fit and I graded it on trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA. H1 FY27 revenue rose 9.9% YoY to ₹325 cr and PAT rose 12.3% to ₹274 cr. Netting out Q1 (₹158 cr, +11.4%) implies Q2 revenue of about ₹167 cr, up roughly 8% YoY with PAT of about ₹139 cr, so growth keeps slowing from the +19% pace of FY25 and early FY26. The reported margin of about 84% is flattered by roughly ₹45 cr a quarter of interest and investment income plus associate profit from IGX. At a trailing P/E of 22.3x (forward 19.6x) and EV/EBITDA of 14.2x, the stock sits mid-range on the 18–28x NBFC/non-bank benchmark and near the 25th percentile of the broad market on P/E and EV/EBITDA, which I grade fair, leaning cheap. It trades near its 52-week low, and the main risk is that slowing volume growth plus regulatory change to the exchange model could stall earnings at a business priced at 8.1x book.

fundamental.thesis: State Bank of India is India's largest lender. At FY26-end it had ₹48.8L cr of advances, ₹59.8L cr of deposits and 55% government ownership. Its Q4FY26 bank KPIs improved: loan growth rose from 15.6% to 16.9% YoY, gross NPA fell from 1.57% to 1.49%, net NPA from 0.47% to 0.39%, and capital adequacy rose to 15.4%. The latest filed quarter (Q1FY27) shows revenue of ₹180,062 cr, up 7.8% YoY, and revenue growth has picked up from +4.9% (Q3FY26) to +7.0% (FY26) to +7.8%. However, Q1FY27 profit is not in the filings data, and the reported NIM jump from 2.55% to 3.03% may reflect a different basis, so treat the margin trend with caution. For valuation I used price-to-book plus ROE, the right yardstick for banks: 1.53× book with a 15.5% ROE sits right at the edge of the desk's cheap band. It also sits at the 57th percentile on P/B among regional bank peers, and the 10.8× trailing P/E (36% below the peer median) doesn't change that, so the grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 3 Nov 2026 and pressure on margins as loans reprice faster than deposits. Provision coverage also slipped from 75.5% to 74.4%, and the desk is underweight Financials in a risk-off market.
